vignette:
Mark describes his life before the attack with a kind of wistful fondness, as if speaking of a different man. For twenty years, he and his wife, Sarah, had a rhythm. He'd open their small, well-loved hardware store at seven, smelling the pleasant mix of sawdust and metal. She'd come by around noon with sandwiches. They built a life on the predictable dependability of things: the morning rush for contractors, the Saturday crowds of DIYers, the quiet evenings at home. He was a man who knew how to fix things. A leaky faucet, a broken fence, a sputtering lawnmower-he took pride in his ability to restore order.

That rhythm shattered fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday. They had gone out for dinner to celebrate a small anniversary, the kind they'd almost forgotten until Sarah remembered that morning. Walking back to their car in the multi-level garage, Mark was telling a story about a customer when two figures emerged from the shadows between concrete pillars. It happened with a disorienting speed that Mark's mind still struggles to process. There was a shout, a shove. He remembers the jarring sound of Sarah's purse hitting the ground, its contents spilling. He remembers one of the men grabbing her arm. But mostly, he remembers the feeling of his own body, frozen. He, who could fix anything, stood paralyzed as his wife was thrown to the ground. The entire event lasted less than a minute before the men were gone, but for Mark, it continues to unspool in an endless, agonizing loop.

In the weeks that followed, he was a model of support. He dealt with the police, the hospital, the insurance. He made sure Sarah, whose wrist was fractured in the fall, was comfortable. He told everyone he was fine, that the important thing was that Sarah was safe. But at night, sleep offered no escape. He'd wake up drenched in sweat, his heart hammering against his ribs, the image of Sarah's frightened face burned into his vision.

Now, the world feels fundamentally unsafe. The bell above the shop door, once a cheerful signal of a customer, now sends a jolt of adrenaline through him. He startles violently if a supplier drops a pallet too loudly in the stockroom. He finds himself scanning the face of every man who enters the store, assessing for threat, his hand subtly tightening on the box cutter in his apron pocket. This constant vigilance is exhausting, leaving him perpetually irritable and on edge. He snapped at a longtime customer for asking too many questions, an act that left him hollow with shame afterward.

He avoids the part of town where the attack happened, taking long, inefficient routes to bypass it entirely. He and Sarah don't go out in the evenings anymore. He insists on triple-checking the locks at home each night, a ritual that provides only a fleeting sense of control. He feels a profound distance from Sarah, a chasm of his own making. When she tries to talk about that night, he changes the subject or retreats into silence. How can he explain the corrosive guilt that eats at him? The persistent, looping thought: *I was right there. I should have done something.* He sees himself as a failure, a man who couldn't protect the one person he was meant to. The pride he once took in his competence and his ability to fix things has been replaced by a deep sense of inadequacy. He spends his days surrounded by tools, yet feels utterly powerless. After closing, he often sits in the dark of his silent shop, the neat rows of hammers and wrenches seeming to mock him, a man whose own life has come undone.
